service.name: Wedding cocktail hour music
service.serviceType: Live music for wedding cocktail hours
service.description: Jazz duo, acoustic duo and solo guitarist bookings for wedding cocktail hours across Denver, the Front Range and the Colorado mountain corridor.

faqs.q: Is there music during cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Yes, at nearly every wedding. The hour between the ceremony and dinner is when guests stand with a first drink and meet each other, and something fills it. Live musicians, a DJ or a playlist through the venue's own system are the three ways it gets filled, and each one feels different to the guests.

faqs.q: Do you need music during cocktail hour?
faqs.a: You need something, and live musicians are the option guests notice. Silence in that hour feels like a gap in the day, because the couple is away for photographs and nothing else is happening yet. A duo at conversation volume covers that hour without asking anyone for their attention.

faqs.q: What kind of music should play during cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Jazz standards and singer-songwriter covers, songs guests recognize without having to name. The repertoire matters less than the level. Upright bass and guitar leaves space in the middle of the sound where conversation sits, which is the actual job of the hour.

faqs.q: How many songs for cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Roughly fifteen to twenty for a 60-minute hour and closer to thirty for 90 minutes, because a standard runs three to four minutes. Live musicians don't work to a count: sets run continuously and tunes stretch or shorten to the crowd.

faqs.q: Will anyone actually notice the music?
faqs.a: Not consciously, and that's the hour going right. Guests notice that the evening felt hosted more than they notice which tunes played. Two musicians playing thirty feet away change how a space feels without becoming the thing being watched.
Yes, that's exactly what the level is set for. Cocktail and dinner sets run 65 to 72 dBA at the nearest table, a volume two people who have just met can talk across without leaning in.

faqs.q: Instrumental or vocals for cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Instrumental, for most of the hour. A voice pulls attention to the words, and guests who are mid-introduction feel that as competition. Upright bass and guitar leaves the middle of the sound clear. Where a wedding wants a voice anyway, a singer can lead the hour and the level comes down to match.

faqs.q: Is a duo overkill for 60 to 70 guests?
faqs.a: No. Two musicians are the right size for that count, holding 65 to 72 dBA across a crowd from twenty at one table to eighty across ten, and a duo can adjust its volume on the spot in a way a bigger build can't.

faqs.q: How long is a wedding cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Sixty minutes is standard. It stretches to 90 when the venue turns one space from ceremony to reception, because guests can't go back in until the flip is done. Added time is booked in 30-minute increments.

faqs.q: Should we book a band or a DJ for cocktail hour?
faqs.a: A duo, for this hour. It reads the crowd, takes a request, and lands at a volume people can talk across. A DJ is the better booking after dinner, carrying the dance floor for hours.

faqs.q: Can one booking cover the cocktail hour and dinner?
faqs.a: Yes. The same two musicians carry cocktails and dinner on the same contract, with sound included and the whole block quoted as one figure for your date. One load-in, one invoice, and the hour never goes silent between sets.
